items.title: Day 2 Overview
items.body:
Day 2 · Unit 1: Whole Numbers

Day 2 Overview

The four operations with whole numbers — adding, subtracting, multiplying, and dividing with carrying, regrouping, and remainders — then a full Unit 1 review, quiz, and test.

Learning Objectives Covered Today

  • Add whole numbers with carrying
  • Add more than two numbers
  • Subtract whole numbers with regrouping
  • Regroup with zeros
  • Multiply whole numbers with carrying
  • Divide by one digit
  • Divide with remainders
  • Divide by larger numbers

How Today Works

Each topic below is a short reading followed by a printable worksheet — the book's own practice problems, done on paper with your calculator. These worksheets are not graded; check your work against the Answer Key dropdown at the bottom of each one before moving to the next topic.

The day ends with the book's own Whole Numbers Review (a self-check with a "which pages to review" chart built in), then the graded Unit 1 Quiz and Unit 1 Test.

Today’s Tasks

  1. Addition with Carrying — read, then Worksheet 4
  2. Addition of More Than Two Numbers — read, then Worksheet 5
  3. Subtraction with Regrouping — read, then Worksheet 6
  4. Regrouping with Zeros — read, then Worksheet 7
  5. Multiplication with Carrying — read, then Worksheet 8
  6. Division by One Digit — read, then Worksheet 9
  7. Division with Remainders — read, then Worksheet 10
  8. Division by Larger Numbers — read, then Worksheet 11
  9. Whole Numbers Review (self-check)
  10. Unit 1 Quiz
  11. Unit 1 Test

items.title: Addition with Carrying — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 11 · CBO Objective: Add whole numbers with carrying

Addition with Carrying

At the ABM Assembly plant there are 857 workers on the day-shift and 268 on the night shift. Find the total number of workers at ABM.

The answer to an addition problem is called the sum or total. When the sum of the digits in a column is a two-digit number, carry the digit at the left to the next column to the left.

Breaking It Down

Carrying is just regrouping: if a column adds up to 10 or more, you're saying “I have more ones than fit in this column, so I'll trade 10 of them for 1 of the next bigger unit.” 15 ones = 1 ten + 5 ones — write the 5, carry the 1 ten into the tens column and add it in there.

Example: 857 + 268 =

Step 1. Add the ones. 7 + 8 = 15. Write 5 under the ones column, and carry the 1 to the tens column.
Step 2. Add the tens. 1 + 5 = 6 and 6 + 6 = 12. Write the 2 under the tens and carry the 1 to the hundreds.
Step 3. Add the hundreds. 1 + 8 = 9 and 9 + 2 = 11.

The total number of workers at ABM is 1,125.

A Second Example (double carry)

456 + 389 =
Ones: 6 + 9 = 15 → write 5, carry 1. Tens: 1 + 5 + 8 = 14 → write 4, carry 1. Hundreds: 1 + 4 + 3 = 8. Answer: 845.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

The most common slip is forgetting to actually add the carried digit once you move to the next column — write it small above the column as a reminder. If a column's total needs a 2-digit carry (like 29 → carry 2, not 1), make sure you carry the full amount, not just “1” out of habit.

Video: Math Antics - Multi-Digit Addition (Math Antics, YouTube)

items.title: Addition of More Than Two Numbers — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 14 · CBO Objective: Add more than two numbers

Addition of More Than Two Numbers

Carlos works in the shipping department of an electrical supply company. For one customer he packed three boxes. One weighed 29 pounds, the second weighed 14 pounds, and the third weighed 7 pounds. Find the total weight of the three boxes.

To add more than two numbers, find the total for each column. The digits in a column can be added in any order.

Breaking It Down

Same carrying rule as before — you're just adding every digit in the column before you carry, instead of only two. It can help to scan for pairs that make 10 first (like spotting 7 + 3) since adding those together first is often faster than working strictly top to bottom.

Example: 29 + 14 + 7 =

Step 1. Line up the numbers and add the digits in the units column. 9 + 4 = 13. Then 13 + 7 = 20. Write 0 in the units column and carry 2 to the tens.
Step 2. Add the digits in the tens column. 2 + 2 = 4. Then 4 + 1 = 5.

The total weight of the boxes is 50 pounds.

A Second Example

148 + 26 + 375 =
Ones: 8 + 6 + 5 = 19 → write 9, carry 1. Tens: 1 + 4 + 2 + 7 = 14 → write 4, carry 1. Hundreds: 1 + 1 + 3 = 5. Answer: 549.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

With four, five, or more rows in a column, it's easy to lose your place and skip or double-count a digit — run your finger or pencil tip down the column as you add. And watch column sums of 20+: you may need to carry a 2, not just a 1.

Same skill, same video

This is the same carrying skill as the previous page — if you want to rewatch it, the Multi-Digit Addition video is on the “Addition with Carrying” reading, or linked again on the Want More Practice? page.

items.title: Subtraction with Regrouping — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 16 · CBO Objective: Subtract whole numbers with regrouping

Subtraction with Regrouping

Carpenters at the ABM Company have to build 85 packing crates. By Wednesday they had finished 39 crates. How many do they have left?

The answer to a subtraction problem is called the difference. When the bottom number in any column is too large to subtract from the top number, you must regroup the top number. You may know this operation as renaming or borrowing.

Breaking It Down

Borrowing is carrying in reverse: when a column doesn't have enough to subtract, you break open 1 unit from the column to its left and turn it into 10 of the smaller unit. Borrow 1 ten → it becomes 10 ones added to what's already there. The column you borrowed from goes down by 1.

Example: 85 − 39 =

Step 1. 9 is too large to subtract from 5. Regroup the top number: take 1 ten from the tens column (8 − 1 = 7) and add it to the units (10 + 5 = 15).
Step 2. Subtract the units. 15 − 9 = 6.
Step 3. Subtract the tens. 7 − 3 = 4.

The carpenters have 46 crates left to build.

A Second Example

63 − 28 =
8 is too big to take from 3, so borrow: 6 tens → 5 tens, and the 3 ones become 13 ones. 13 − 8 = 5. Then 5 tens − 2 tens = 3. Answer: 35.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

The classic early-learner error is subtracting the smaller digit from the larger one regardless of which is on top (e.g. doing 9 − 5 instead of borrowing, just because 9 is bigger) — always check whether the TOP digit is big enough first. And after you borrow from a column, don't forget to actually reduce that column by 1 before you get to it.

Video: Math Antics - Multi-Digit Subtraction (Math Antics, YouTube)

items.title: Regrouping with Zeros — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 18 · CBO Objective: Regroup with zeros

Regrouping with Zeros

Imani had $904 in her savings account. She withdrew $356 to buy new winter clothes. How much did she have left in her account?

To regroup with zeros, look at the first digit in the top number that is not zero.

Breaking It Down

Normally you borrow from the very next column over. But if that column is a zero, there's nothing there to borrow — so you have to reach further left to the first non-zero digit, borrow from it, and then “cascade” that borrow back down through every zero in between (each zero becomes a 9, except the very last one, which becomes 10 and combines with the ones column).

Example: 904 − 356 =

Step 1. You cannot subtract 6 from 4. Take 1 hundred from the hundreds column (9 − 1 = 8). You now have 10 tens in the tens column.
Step 2. Take 1 ten from the 10 in the tens column (10 − 1 = 9) and add it to the units (10 + 4 = 14).
Step 3. Subtract the units. 14 − 6 = 8.
Step 4. Subtract the tens. 9 − 5 = 4.
Step 5. Subtract the hundreds. 8 − 3 = 5.

Imani had $548 left in her account.

A Second Example (single zero)

500 − 247 =
The tens column is 0, so reach to the hundreds: 5 → 4, and that 1 hundred becomes 10 tens. Now borrow 1 ten for the ones: 10 tens → 9 tens, and the ones become 10. 10 − 7 = 3. 9 − 4 = 5. 4 − 2 = 2. Answer: 253.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

With more than one zero in a row (like 4,000 − 1,256), the cascade has to pass through every zero — stopping the borrow too early is the #1 error here. Each zero you pass through becomes a 9; only the very last one becomes 10.

Same skill, same video

This builds directly on the Multi-Digit Subtraction video from the previous page — rewatch it if the zero-cascade felt shaky, and try the practice problems on the Want More Practice? page.

items.title: Multiplication with Carrying — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 20 · CBO Objective: Multiply whole numbers with carrying

Multiplication with Carrying

The shipping department at Ace Electrical sent out 29 crates of motor parts. Each crate weighed 76 pounds. Find the total weight of the shipment.

The answer to a multiplication problem is called the product. When you multiply two digits, the product is often a two-digit number. You must carry the left digit to the next number you are multiplying. Then add the digit you carry to the next product.

Breaking It Down

Multiplying by a 2-digit number is really two smaller multiplications added together, called partial products: first multiply by the ones digit, then multiply by the tens digit (writing that second row shifted one place to the left, since you're really multiplying by a number of tens). Add the two partial products for your final answer.

Example: 76 × 29 =

Step 1. 9 × 6 = 54. Write 4 in the units column, and carry 5 to the next column.
Step 2. 9 × 7 = 63. Add the 5 you carried: 63 + 5 = 68.
Step 3. 2 × 6 = 12. Write 2 in the tens column, carry the 1 to the next column.
Step 4. 2 × 7 = 14. Add the 1 you carried: 14 + 1 = 15.
Step 5. Add the partial products.

The total weight of the shipment was 2,204 pounds.

A Second Example (with partial products shown)

58 × 43 =
Partial product 1 (58 × 3): 174. Partial product 2 (58 × 4, shifted one place left because it's really ×40): 2,320. Add: 174 + 2,320 = 2,494.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

The #1 error is forgetting to shift the second partial product one place to the left (or forgetting its placeholder zero) — that shift is what makes it ×40 instead of ×4. Also watch for carrying mistakes inside a single partial product, same as regular multi-digit multiplication.

Video: Math Antics - Multi-Digit Multiplication Pt 1 (Math Antics, YouTube)

items.title: Division by One Digit — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 22-23 · CBO Objective: Divide by one digit

Division by One Digit

Serena has a part-time job at a convenience store. She makes $6 an hour. Last month she made $504. How many hours did she work?

The answer to a division problem is called the quotient. To find a quotient, repeat these four steps until you complete the problem: 1. Divide. 2. Multiply. 3. Subtract and compare. 4. Bring down the next number.

Breaking It Down

Long division is really a sequence of small “how many times does this fit?” questions, worked one digit at a time from left to right. Each round follows the same 4-step cycle (Divide → Multiply → Subtract → Bring down) until there are no more digits left to bring down.

Example: Divide 6 into 504.

Step 1. Divide: 6 goes into 50 eight times. Write 8 above the tens place.
Step 2. Multiply: 8 × 6 = 48. Write 48 under 50.
Step 3. Subtract: 50 − 48 = 2. Compare to be sure 2 is less than 6.
Step 4. Bring down the next number: 4.
Step 5. Divide: 6 goes into 24 four times. Write 4 above the units place.
Step 6. Multiply: 4 × 6 = 24. Write 24 under 24.
Step 7. Subtract: 24 − 24 = 0. Compare: 0 is less than 6.

Serena worked 84 hours.

Writing every step is called long division. In short division you write only the answer and the number you get by subtracting.

A Second Example

Divide 4 into 372.
4 goes into 37 nine times (9×4=36, remainder 1). Bring down the 2 → 12. 4 goes into 12 three times exactly. Answer: 93.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Writing the quotient digit above the wrong column is the most common slip — each digit you write goes directly above the digit you just brought down. And don't skip bringing down the next digit before continuing; that's what tells you when the problem is finished.

Video: Math Antics - Long Division (Math Antics, YouTube)

items.title: Division with Remainders — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 24 · CBO Objective: Divide with remainders

Division with Remainders

How many buckets, each containing 4 quarts of paint, can Alan fill from a vat that contains 387 quarts of paint?

If you do not get zero in the last subtraction step of a division problem, you will have a remainder.

Breaking It Down

A remainder is simply whatever's left over that doesn't divide evenly. What you do with a remainder in a real business problem depends on context: if you're asking “how many full buckets,” you drop the remainder (it's the leftover paint, not another bucket). But if the question were “how many buckets do I need to buy to hold ALL the paint,” you'd round up even with a remainder, since a partly-full bucket still counts as one you need.

In this unit, just report the remainder as-is (written “r” followed by the leftover number) unless a problem specifically asks you to interpret it.

Example: 387 ÷ 4 = 96r3

Alan can fill 96 buckets. There will be 3 quarts left over.

If a division problem is written with the ÷ sign, rewrite the problem using the long-division bracket before dividing.

A Second Example

260 ÷ 7 =
7 goes into 26 three times (3×7=21, remainder 5). Bring down the 0 → 50. 7 goes into 50 seven times (7×7=49, remainder 1). Answer: 37r1.

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Your remainder should always be smaller than the number you're dividing by — if it isn't, that's a sign your last “divide” step guessed too low and you need to go one higher. And don't forget to write the remainder at all — “96” and “96r3” are different answers.

Same skill, same video

This is the same long-division process from the previous page, just with problems that don't divide evenly — rewatch the Long Division video there if you need it.

items.title: Division by Larger Numbers — Reading
items.body:
Day 2 · Unit 1 Reading

Book pages: 26 · CBO Objective: Divide by larger numbers

Division by Larger Numbers

Sonny borrowed $2,976. He is paying back $62 a month. How many months will he need to repay the entire loan?

To divide by two-digit and three-digit numbers, you must estimate how many times one number divides into another number. When you estimate, you make a guess.

Breaking It Down

Dividing by a bigger number means you usually can't just “know” the answer from memorized facts — you estimate (often by looking at just the lead digits), then check your estimate by multiplying back out, and adjust up or down if it was wrong. This estimate-check-adjust loop is the whole skill; don't expect to get every estimate right on the first try.

Example: Divide 2,976 by 62.

Step 1. Estimate how many times 62 divides into 297: ask how many times 6 divides into 29 (29 ÷ 6 = 4 plus a remainder). Write 4 above the 7.
Step 2. Multiply: 4 × 62 = 248. Write 248 under 297.
Step 3. Subtract: 297 − 248 = 49, and compare: 49 is less than 62.
Step 4. Bring down the next number: 6.
Step 5. Estimate how many times 62 divides into 496: ask how many times 6 goes into 49 (49 ÷ 6 = 8 plus a remainder). Write 8 above the 6.
Step 6. Multiply: 8 × 62 = 496. Write 496 under 496.
Step 7. Subtract: 496 − 496 = 0.
Step 8. Check: 48 × 62 = 2,976.

Sonny will need 48 months to repay the loan.

Sometimes your first estimate will be wrong. Work with a pencil and a good eraser. Decide if your estimate is too small or too large and try again.

A Second Example (adjusting an estimate)

1,464 ÷ 24 =
Estimate: 24 into 146 — try 6 (6×24=144, remainder 2, works). Bring down the 4 → 24. 24 goes into 24 exactly once. Answer: 61. (If you'd first guessed 7, 7×24=168 is too big — that's the “adjust down” moment this skill is all about.)

Common Mistakes to Avoid

Always verify an estimate by multiplying it back out before moving on — if the remainder you get is bigger than the divisor, your estimate was too low and needs to go up by 1 (or more). Don't just accept the first guess without checking.

Video: Math Antics - Long Division with 2-Digit Divisors (Math Antics, YouTube)
